Abstract INTRODUCTION Identifying at‐risk individuals and selecting sensitive cognitive outcome measures are critical for designing efficient clinical trials targeting early Alzheimer's disease (AD) stages. METHODS We compared amyloid beta (Aβ)‐positron emission tomography (PET), plasma tau phosphorylated at threonine 217 (p‐tau217), Aβ42/40, and p‐tau217/Aβ42‐related decline across neuropsychological and functional measures in 225 individuals (176 cognitively unimpaired (CU), 49 with mild cognitive impairment (MCI). Johnson–Neyman analysis identified the biomarkers, which were used as trial inclusion criteria to estimate sample sizes needed to detect a 30% slowing across cognitive outcomes. RESULTS In the CU, using combined plasma Aβ42/40 and p‐tau217 cut‐offs for eligibility yielded the lowest sample size estimates for a comprehensive multidomain cognitive composite score, whereas sample sizes were higher for all other inclusion criteria based on single biomarkers. In MCI, estimates were substantially lower and less variable across most inclusion criteria and outcome measures. DISCUSSION These findings highlight the need for careful consideration of outcome measures, baseline diagnosis, and inclusion criteria, given their substantial effect on sample size estimation in trials. Highlights Aβ SUVR, plasma p‐tau217, and the p‐tau217/Aβ42 ratio predicted decline across multiple cognitive domains. Using cohort‐specific biomarker cutoffs, sample size estimates were similar for p‐tau217 combined with Aβ42/40 or Aβ SUVR. A multidomain composite best detected AD‐related decline. 21 : e70802 . 10.1002/alz.70802 1 BACKGROUND Alzheimer's disease (AD) is characterized by the appearance of neuropathological changes while affected individuals are still asymptomatic. 1 The aggregation and accumulation of amyloid beta (Aβ) peptides into extracellular plaques in the brain are among the earliest detectable pathophysiological abnormalities, starting about two decades prior to the onset of clinical symptoms. 2 , 3 However, subtle decline in cognitive performance related to Aβ deposits in the brain can be detected much earlier, 4 providing an early indication of an increased risk of developing clinical AD. Cerebral Aβ plaques can be reliably quantified using positron emission tomography (PET) imaging, 5 and recent technical advances have enabled successful quantification of AD biomarkers in blood. 6 The plasma Aβ42/40 ratio and levels of tau phosphorylated at threonine 217 (p‐tau217) are among the most promising blood‐based biomarkers that distinguish abnormal from normal Aβ status, 7 , 8 , 9 predict Aβ accumulation, 10 and show high performance in predicting cognitive decline. 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 These biomarkers hold significant potential as (pre)screening tools for clinical trials to identify individuals with a high likelihood of Aβ pathology 13 and to enrich the clinical trial population with individuals at increased risk of cognitive decline. 6 , 15 Such a prescreening strategy enhances statistical power and reduces the sample size needed to detect a treatment effect. Another key factor affecting sample size in AD trials is the ability to measure cognitive change sensitively and reliably using optimized outcome measures. Outcome measures that integrate cognition and function, such as the Clinical Dementia Rating–Sum of Boxes (CDR‐SoB), have been widely used in past and ongoing AD trials. However, as clinical trials increasingly target Aβ‐positive, cognitively unimpaired (CU) individuals, 16 purely cognitive outcome measures may now be more appropriate and informative. Among these, multidomain cognitive composites are currently considered the most sensitive tools for detecting the subtle, gradual decline observed in preclinical and early AD. 17 , 18 The Preclinical Alzheimer Cognitive Composite (PACC) is one such measure that has been developed to assess the effects of solanezumab – a monoclonal antibody targeting monomeric Aβ – in the Anti‐Amyloid Treatment in Asymptomatic Alzheimer's Disease (A4) trial. 19 , 20 While the PACC is now widely used in research and clinical trials, previous studies indicate that cognitive decline as measured with the PACC is minimal in individuals with intermediate levels of Aβ. 21 , 22 Hence, there remains a need to refine cognitive outcome measures to enable the detection of subtle decline in the very early stages of the disease. The choice of outcome measure, along with the clinical disease stage of the target population, may also influence which biomarker is most relevant for predicting disease progression. 23 Together, these considerations highlight the need for a strategic, disease‐stage‐specific approach to outcome measure and biomarker selection in the design of AD clinical trials. In this study, we investigated how disease stage, cognitive outcome measures, and biomarkers used to predict disease progression interact to influence the sample size required to detect treatment effects in hypothetical clinical trials. We first compared the performance of Aβ‐PET, plasma Aβ42/40, plasma p‐tau217, and plasma p‐tau217/Aβ42 in predicting cognitive and functional decline over time in a community‐based sample of older adults. We then investigated how enrollment based on combinations of PET and plasma biomarkers, along with baseline cognitive status and the chosen cognitive outcome measure, influenced sample size estimates required to detect treatment effects.

We then investigated how enrollment based on combinations of PET and plasma biomarkers, along with baseline cognitive status and the chosen cognitive outcome measure, influenced sample size estimates required to detect treatment effects. 2 METHODS 2.1 Study population Participants were enrolled in the IDcog study, 24 , 25 a longitudinal, community‐based cohort study of cognitive change conducted at the Center for Prevention and Dementia Therapy at the Institute for Regenerative Medicine, University of Zurich, Switzerland. Participants were recruited via newspaper advertisements. To be eligible for enrollment in the study, participants had to be at least 50 years of age and German‐speaking. Individuals with comorbid conditions that could interfere with cognitive assessments or with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and PET procedures were excluded. Individuals with dementia, non‐silent strokes, and cardiovascular disease resulting in cognitive impairment, clinically significant depression, evidence of cognitive impairment primarily attributable to a medical condition other than potential AD pathology, such as medication use, substance abuse, or heart failure were also excluded. The diagnosis of CU or mild cognitive impairment (MCI) was established during a clinical consensus conference, involving at least one experienced clinician and a neuropsychologist, in accordance with established diagnostic guidelines. 26 Specifically, a diagnosis of MCI required (1) a subjective cognitive complaint reported either by the participant or by someone familiar with them; (2) objective evidence of cognitive impairment, defined as a performance at least 1.5 standard deviations below the norm (z‐score < −1.5) on at least one cognitive test relevant to the affected domain; (3) documented evidence of cognitive decline based on medical history; and (4) preserved ability to perform activities of daily living. RESEARCH IN CONTEXT Systematic review : Relevant articles were identified using Google Scholar and by reviewing cited works. Prior studies suggested that plasma p‐tau217 could predict cognitive decline even in preclinical stages. However, a comprehensive comparison between plasma and PET biomarkers is lacking, and the most sensitive cognitive tasks and composite scores for tracking decline remain unclear. Interpretation : Combining plasma p‐tau217 and Aβ42/40 improves the identification of individuals most likely to experience cognitive decline compared to single biomarker cutoffs. Multidomain cognitive composites are particularly sensitive to tracking decline, particularly in preclinical AD, supporting their use in early AD trials to increase sensitivity and reduce sample sizes. Trial screening and outcome measures may be tailored to the target population. Future directions : Further refinement of participant selection and outcome measures could further reduce sample size requirements. Standardized and validated plasma biomarker thresholds are needed to identify individuals at increased risk. At baseline, the cohort consisted of 233 participants, all of whom underwent Aβ‐PET imaging and cognitive assessments. Tau‐PET was not included in the current analysis due to limited availability, with data accessible for less than half of the participants. Participants were followed longitudinally with cognitive assessments every year. At each assessment, participants underwent clinical evaluation and neuropsychological testing. In this study, we included participants who had at least one neuropsychological assessment after their baseline visit. All participants gave written informed consent. 2.2 Aβ‐PET imaging and processing Dynamic Aβ‐PET images were acquired from 80 to 110 min after injection using approximately 140 MBq [18F]‐flutemetamol. 27 A global Aβ standardized uptake value ratio (SUVR) was calculated from the averaged frames acquired between 85 and 105 min after injection (four frames of 5 min each) in a cortical composite region of interest, which included the bilateral frontal, temporal, and parietal cortices and posterior and anterior cingulate gyrus normalized to the uptake in the cerebellar gray matter. For descriptive purposes, we report the number of individuals with a Centiloid > 12, which marks the transition from the absence of pathology to the onset of subtle pathological changes. 28 2.3 Plasma Aβ and p‐tau217 measurement At the baseline visit, blood was collected from each participant in ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) tubes (Vacutainer EDTA Tubes, BD), inverted 10 times, and centrifuged (1620 × g, 12 min, 6°C) to obtain plasma samples. Aliquots of 3 mL plasma were immediately frozen at −80°C and stored at the Institute for Regenerative Medicine, University of Zurich, Zurich, Switzerland. Plasma AD biomarker analysis was conducted at the Clinical Neurochemistry Laboratory, University of Gothenburg, Mölndal, Sweden. In brief, quantifications of plasma Aβ42 and Aβ40 were performed with a customized Neurology 4‐plex E Simoa platform (Quanterix). Plasma p‐tau217 was measured using an in‐house Simoa‐based assay developed at the University of Gothenburg. 29 Plasma biomarker levels below the limit of quantitation (LOQ) were set at LOQ/2 according to standard approaches for left‐censored LOQ data. 30 P‐tau217 was below the LOQ in 96 participants (43%; CU: 78 [44%]; MCI: 18 [37%]) and was not available in four participants (two CU, two MCI).

30 P‐tau217 was below the LOQ in 96 participants (43%; CU: 78 [44%]; MCI: 18 [37%]) and was not available in four participants (two CU, two MCI). 2.4 Cognitive measures Functional changes, quality of life, and cognitive performance were assessed during annual visits. The neuropsychological examination was usually carried out in the morning and lasted around 90 min with a short break after 45 min. The CDR‐SoB was assessed as a measure of combined cognitive and functional outcomes, and the Instrumental Activities of Daily Living S1 (IADL) questionnaire was evaluated as a measure of functional outcome. However, due to missing data and limited variability, which made meaningful statistical analysis difficult, changes in the IADL are visualized in Figure S1 but not further analyzed statistically. Episodic memory was measured using scores of learning (sum of scores from trials 1 to 5), delayed recall, and recognition (hits minus false alarms) of the German version of the Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test S2 (RAVLT) as well as wordlist learning (total of trials 1 to 3), delayed recall, and delayed recall of figures (mean score of four figures) of the Consortium to Establish a Registry for Alzheimer's Disease S3 (CERAD) test battery. Semantic memory was measured by category fluency (animal names, S4 correct new words in second minute). Language function was measured using the Boston Naming Test. S5 Working memory was measured using the Corsi Block (backward) task. S6 Executive functions were measured using Part B of the Trail Making Test S7 (TMT‐B), the ratio of TMT‐B and TMT‐A, Stroop task S8 III (color‐word), letter fluency S9 (s‐words, correct new words in third minute), and the Digit Span S10 (backward). Visuospatial construction was measured using the figure copy tasks in the CERAD test battery (mean score for four figures) and the Rey Complex Figure Task. S11 Processing speed was measured using Part A of the TMT and Stroop task I (word). Global cognitive performance was assessed using the standard version of the Mini‐Mental State Examination S12 (MMSE) included in the CERAD battery. The means and standard deviations of the CU sample at baseline were used to calculate z‐scores for all time points. Where necessary, we reversed the z‐scores so that a higher score represents better performance across all tests. For the second part of our analysis, we created three composite scores. We created a modified version of the Preclinical Alzheimer's Cognitive Composite 5 (mPACC5). 31 As in previous studies, 32 , 33 this version included the MMSE, CERAD delayed recall, RAVLT delayed recall, TMT‐B, and category fluency (animals, correct words in first minute). In addition, we created a global composite score incorporating all neuropsychological test scores mentioned above. Beyond these predefined composites, we used a post hoc score derived from our initial analysis of individual tests, with the assumption that this score would optimally capture AD‐related decline in the present cohort, providing a best‐case scenario for our power calculations. This score averaged the tasks that showed significant plasma p‐tau217‐related decline after false discovery rate (FDR) correction, including CERAD learning, CERAD delayed recall (words and figures), category fluency, TMT‐A and TMT‐B, Stroop I, and the MMSE. As this score combines memory, executive function, and processing speed tasks, we refer to this composite as the MEM‐EF‐PS score. All composite scores were calculated by averaging the standardized z‐scores and were then again standardized using the means and standard deviations of the CU sample at baseline. 2.5 Statistical analysis Baseline differences between CU and MCI groups were analyzed with t tests, Wilcoxon rank‐sum tests, or χ 2 tests as appropriate. We ran a series of linear mixed‐effects models with subject‐specific random intercept and, when models converged, random slopes to examine the longitudinal associations between baseline Aβ SUVR, plasma Aβ42/40, p‐tau217, and p‐tau217/Aβ42 with decline in our cognitive outcome measures. All biomarkers were investigated in separate linear mixed‐effects models. Models included the fixed effects of biomarker and time (years since baseline) and biomarker‐by‐time interaction, as well as the covariates baseline age, sex, and years of education

ts, Wilcoxon rank‐sum tests, or χ 2 tests as appropriate. We ran a series of linear mixed‐effects models with subject‐specific random intercept and, when models converged, random slopes to examine the longitudinal associations between baseline Aβ SUVR, plasma Aβ42/40, p‐tau217, and p‐tau217/Aβ42 with decline in our cognitive outcome measures. All biomarkers were investigated in separate linear mixed‐effects models. Models included the fixed effects of biomarker and time (years since baseline) and biomarker‐by‐time interaction, as well as the covariates baseline age, sex, and years of education. For simplicity and ease of result visualization and comparison, we assumed a linear decline across all cognitive tasks. Model assumptions were visually assessed using residual plots. Given the relative robustness of linear mixed‐effects models to violations of normality and heteroscedasticity, 34 we adopted a relatively lenient criterion for evaluating these assumptions. This also ensured comparability across different outcomes, biomarker predictors, and with previous studies. 35 , 36 To enable direct comparison between models, biomarker measures were z‐transformed using the mean and standard deviation of the total cohort. Correction for multiple comparisons was performed using FDR adjustment. We also tested models that combined two biomarkers in the same model to determine if these were independently associated with outcome measures. These analyses were conducted in the total cohort combining CU and MCI participants as well as in the two subsamples of participants with a baseline diagnosis of CU or MCI. Differences in cognitive decline between baseline CU and MCI participants were investigated in models adjusted for age, sex, and years of education. Progression from CU to MCI or from MCI to dementia was not analyzed due to the small number of cases: only 11 CU participants progressed to MCI, and only three MCI participants progressed to dementia (all diagnosed with AD). Trajectories of the CDR‐SoB were investigated using linear mixed‐effects models in which time was modeled using natural cubic splines with two degrees of freedom, as previously suggested. 37 Biomarker levels were categorized into quartiles for this analysis. We applied the Johnson–Neyman technique 38 to determine thresholds at which Aβ‐PET, plasma Aβ42/40, p‐tau217, and p‐tau217/Aβ42 began to predict the slope of cognitive change in the three composite scores. The Centiloid threshold was of primary interest due to its comparability with prior research, but thresholds for plasma biomarkers were also examined as these were subsequently used as trial inclusion criteria in our sample size analyses. Finally, we conducted sample‐size analyses to determine the number of participants needed to detect treatment effects across different trial inclusion criteria and the three cognitive composite scores as primary outcomes. We used the lowest thresholds estimated in the Johnson–Neyman analysis to define biomarker positivity for trial inclusion. Thresholds were used from the total cohort as these were considered more reliable due to the larger sample size. In a sensitivity analysis, we repeated the sample size calculation using the diagnosis‐specific biomarker thresholds. Linear mixed‐effects models, with time as the sole fixed effect, were used to estimate the mean and standard deviations of change in biomarker‐positive individuals. All models included participant‐specific random intercepts but not random slopes. The estimated parameters were then used to calculate 39 the sample size required to detect 30% slowing in mean rate of cognitive decline over a hypothetical 3‐year clinical trial with a 12‐month assessment interval, 80% power, 40 and a significance level of α = 0.05. To contextualize the decline in CU participants, we calculated the difference between the mean composite score after 3 years in the biomarker‐positive CU participants and the mean baseline score in the MCI group. 32 Additional sample size analyses assessed the sample size based on varying trial durations and biomarker thresholds for eligibility. For both Centiloid and plasma p‐tau217, we selected three thresholds: Centiloid > 14, > 24, and > 34 and p‐tau217 > 1.53, > 1.78, and > 2.03 pg/mL. The lowest thresholds were based on the Johnson–Neyman analysis, while the higher cutoffs were chosen arbitrarily to yield comparable minimum number of participants meeting the criteria. These increasing thresholds primarily aimed to illustrate the impact of more stringent inclusion criteria on sample size estimates. Sample size calculations were not performed for the CDR‐SoB because only a few individuals demonstrated meaningful and consistent progression on this measure. Analyses were performed in R version 4.4.1 using the packages lme4 (version 1.1.35.5) and effects (version 4.2.2) for linear mixed‐effects models, interactions (version 1.1.5) for the Johnson–Neyman analysis, and the “lmmpower” function in the longpower (version 1.0.27) package for the power analysis. 3 RESULTS 3.1 Cohort characteristics Of the 233 participants enrolled in the IDcog cohort, 225 participants had at least one follow‐up neuropsychological assessment and were included in this study. At baseline, these participants were aged 66 ± 8.2 years, 105 (46.7%) were female, 49 (21.8%) had a diagnosis of MCI, and 72 (32%) had a Centiloid > 12. Table 2 summarizes the baseline characteristics for the total sample and the CU and MCI subsamples. Compared to CU, participants with MCI were older ( p < 0.001) and had fewer years of education ( p = 0.03), lower MMSE scores ( p < 0.001), higher Aβ SUVR ( p = 0.01), and higher plasma p‐tau217 ( p = 0.005). There were no group differences in the distribution of sex ( p = 0.16), apolipoprotein E ( APOE ) ε4 carriers ( p = 0.28), and Aβ positivity ( p = 0.19). The majority of MCI participants ( n = 40, 82%) were diagnosed with amnestic MCI. In the total cohort, Aβ‐PET exhibited a modest correlation with plasma biomarkers (Aβ42/40: Spearman's rho = −0.35; p‐tau217: rho = 0.35; p‐tau217/Aβ42: rho = 0.39; all p < 0.001). Correlations were higher in the MCI (Aβ42/40: rho = −0.54; p‐tau217: rho = 0.68; p‐tau217/Aβ42: rho = 0.69; all p < 0.001) compared to the CU subsample (Aβ42/40: rho = −0.26; p‐tau217: rho = 0.22; p‐tau217/Aβ42: rho = 0.28; all p < 0.001) (Figure S2 ). 3.2 Longitudinal decline in cognitive outcome measures We first investigated whether baseline levels of Aβ‐PET, Aβ42/40, p‐tau217, and p‐tau217/Aβ42 predicted decline in individual neuropsychological tasks. At baseline, associations between biomarkers and outcome measures were largely absent (Figure S3 ). The following sections summarize the results of the linear mixed‐effects models examining biomarker‐by‐time interactions as predictors of longitudinal cognitive decline for the total cohort and the baseline CU and baseline MCI subsamples. 2 Longitudinal decline in cognitive outcome measures We first investigated whether baseline levels of Aβ‐PET, Aβ42/40, p‐tau217, and p‐tau217/Aβ42 predicted decline in individual neuropsychological tasks. At baseline, associations between biomarkers and outcome measures were largely absent (Figure S3 ). The following sections summarize the results of the linear mixed‐effects models examining biomarker‐by‐time interactions as predictors of longitudinal cognitive decline for the total cohort and the baseline CU and baseline MCI subsamples. The adjusted standardized coefficients of all biomarkers are presented in Figure 1A–C . Detailed estimates including 95% confidence intervals (CIs) and p values are provided in Table S1 . 3.2.1 Total cohort In the total cohort, stronger AD biomarker abnormality was associated with faster cognitive decline across multiple domains, including episodic memory (CERAD learning, RAVLT delayed recall, CERAD delayed recall for both words and figures), semantic memory (category fluency), language (Boston Naming Test), executive function (TMT‐B), processing speed (TMT‐A, Stroop I), and visuospatial construction (Rey Complex Figure Task) (Figure 1A ). The strongest decline associated with Aβ SUVR ( β = −0.11, 95% CI: −0.16 to −0.06) and plasma p‐tau217/Aβ42 ( β = −0.10, 95% CI: −0.15 to −0.05) was observed in CERAD delayed recall (figures). For plasma p‐tau217, the strongest decline was seen in CERAD delayed recall ( β = −0.10, 95% CI: −0.14 to −0.07). Overall, all three biomarkers were consistently associated with marked and comparable decline in CERAD delayed recall (both words and figures) and TMT‐B performance. In contrast, plasma Aβ42/40 was not significantly associated with cognitive decline in most domains. Notably, all four biomarkers were significantly associated with worsening MMSE scores over time. Based on the number of cognitive tasks showing significant biomarker‐related decline after FDR correction, plasma Aβ42/40 demonstrated the weakest performance, predicting decline in only two tasks. In contrast, plasma p‐tau predicted decline in eight tasks, plasma p‐tau217/Aβ42 in seven tasks, and Aβ SUVR in six tasks. 3.2.2 Baseline CU In the baseline CU subgroup, performance of biomarkers in predicting decline was limited (Figure 1B ). Significant biomarker‐related decline was observed in episodic memory (CERAD learning and delayed recall), executive function (TMT‐B and TMT‐B/TMT‐A), and language (Boston Naming Test), though these associations did not remain significant after FDR correction. The strongest decline associated with Aβ SUVR was observed in CERAD learning ( β = −0.06, 95% CI: −0.11 to −0.02), while plasma p‐tau217 showed its greatest association with decline in CERAD delayed recall ( β = −0.07, 95% CI: −0.11 to −0.02). Additionally, lower plasma Aβ42/40 predicted faster decline in the Boston Naming Test ( β = 0.04, 95% CI: 0.00 to 0.05). When considering uncorrected p values, higher Aβ SUVR was associated with decline in four tasks, while higher plasma p‐tau217 and lower Aβ42/40 were each associated with decline in one task. Plasma p‐tau217/Aβ42 did not significantly predict decline in any task.

Plasma p‐tau217/Aβ42 did not significantly predict decline in any task. 3.2.3 Baseline MCI In the baseline MCI subgroup, AD biomarker‐related decline was observed in the same cognitive domains and tasks as in the total cohort (Figure 1C ). The main difference was that these associations were more pronounced, and significant biomarker‐related decline was additionally observed in the RAVLT learning task. For Aβ SUVR ( β = −0.14, 95% CI: −0.22 to −0.06), plasma p‐tau217 ( β = −0.17, 95% CI: −0.24 to −0.09), and plasma p‐tau217/Aβ42 ( β = −0.17, 95% CI: −0.24 to −0.10) the strongest decline was observed in the TMT‐B. For plasma Aβ42/40, the strongest decline was seen in CERAD delayed recall ( β = 0.13, 95% CI: 0.05 to 0.21). After FDR correction, p‐tau217 predicted decline in nine tasks, Aβ SUVR in six tasks, p‐tau217/Aβ42 in five tasks, and Aβ42/Aβ40 in three tasks. 3.2.4 Sensitivity analyses The results were highly similar when we excluded participants with p‐tau217 measurements below the limit of detection (Figure S4 ). When Aβ‐PET and plasma Aβ42/40 were included as predictors in the same linear mixed‐effects models, Aβ‐PET demonstrated stronger predictive power for cognitive decline across nearly all tasks (Figure S5 ). Similarly, when plasma Aβ42/40 and p‐tau217 were combined in the same models, p‐tau217 was the main predictor of decline (Figure S6 ). Notably, for several neuropsychological measures that previously showed associations with Aβ SUVR and p‐tau217, significant associations with both biomarkers were also observed when they were combined in the same model (Figure S7 ). A similar observation was made when Aβ SUVR and p‐tau217/Aβ42 were included in the same model (Figure S8 ). When examining the effect of baseline diagnosis on outcome measures, we found that MCI participants performed worse across most tests at baseline (Table S2 ). However, compared to CU participants, MCI participants showed significantly faster declines only in CERAD delayed recall (figures) ( β = −0.18, 95% CI: −0.30 to −0.07), TMT Part A ( β = −0.09, 95% CI: −0.18 to −0.02), and Stroop I ( β = −0.09, 95% CI: −0.16 to −0.02). Conversely, MCI participants exhibited less decline in RAVLT recognition ( β = 0.15, 95% CI: 0.04 to 0.26) and in TMT B/A ( β = 0.10, 95% CI: 0.00 to 0.21) compared to CU participants.

Conversely, MCI participants exhibited less decline in RAVLT recognition ( β = 0.15, 95% CI: 0.04 to 0.26) and in TMT B/A ( β = 0.10, 95% CI: 0.00 to 0.21) compared to CU participants. 3.3 Longitudinal increase in CDR‐SoB A worsening in CDR‐SoB was predominantly observed in the quartile representing the highest biomarker abnormality (Q4) at baseline. This trend was consistent across all four biomarkers (Figure 2A–D ). 3.4 Biomarker threshold for predicting cognitive decline We then used Johnson–Neyman analysis to identify the biomarker thresholds at which they significantly predicted cognitive changes across the three composite scores. Results for Aβ SUVR are presented in Figure 3 , and results for plasma Aβ42/40 (Figure S9 ), p‐tau217 (Figure S10 ), and p‐tau217/Aβ42 (Figure S11 ) are provided in the Supplementary Materials. 3.4.1 Total cohort In the total cohort, the lowest threshold at which Aβ‐PET significantly predicted decline was observed for the MEM‐EF‐PS composite (SUVR 1.27, ∼14 CL), followed by the global composite score (SUVR 1.13, ∼18 CL) and the mPACC5 (SUVR 1.43, ∼30 CL). A similar pattern was observed in the MCI group, though differences in estimated sample sizes were less pronounced and overall sample size requirements were substantially lower compared to the CU group. 4 DISCUSSION In this study, we compared Aβ‐PET, plasma Aβ42/40, plasma p‐tau217, and plasma p‐tau217/Aβ42 as predictors of decline over 3.5 years in a community‐based cohort and examined their implications for clinical trial sample size estimates. In general, we found that enrolling individuals based on a combined cutoff approach of plasma Aβ42/40 and p‐tau217 or Aβ‐PET and plasma p‐tau217 biomarkers alongside cognitive assessments that span multiple domains resulted in the lowest sample size estimates. This strategy was effective in both CU and MCI samples but was especially advantageous in preclinical AD, where it substantially reduced sample size requirements. In contrast, sample sizes in MCI remained comparatively low across most inclusion criteria and outcome measures. Overall, our results illustrate how outcome measures, biomarker inclusion thresholds, and the baseline diagnosis of the target population interact to shape sample size estimates in trials aiming to detect early AD‐related cognitive decline.

Overall, our results illustrate how outcome measures, biomarker inclusion thresholds, and the baseline diagnosis of the target population interact to shape sample size estimates in trials aiming to detect early AD‐related cognitive decline. The cognitive tests sensitive to biomarker‐related decline were mostly the same across all investigated AD biomarkers. Decline was primarily observed in tasks assessing memory, executive function, and processing speed. However, p‐tau217‐related decline extended to semantic (animal fluency) and visuospatial‐construction (Rey Complex Figure Copy) tasks, where other biomarkers showed no decline. Overall, p‐tau217 slightly outperformed Aβ SUVR in predicting cognitive decline in the total cohort and the MCI subsample. In contrast, in the CU subsample, Aβ SUVR was a slightly stronger predictor, predicting decline in four tasks (CERAD learning and delayed recall, TMT‐B, and TMT‐B/TMT‐A) compared top‐tau217, which predicted decline in only one, CERAD delayed recall. Episodic memory is particularly vulnerable to early AD pathology, and its decline is a core feature of typical amnestic AD. 41 , 42 Some studies reported a specific early decline in episodic memory, 43 , 44 while others observed decline across multiple cognitive domains. 45 Our findings tend to support the latter. We found that in CU participants, AD biomarker‐related cognitive changes were primarily observed in episodic memory and executive function tasks. Interestingly, although the decline in CU participants was limited to episodic memory and executive function, combining these tasks into a composite score would not result in an earlier detection of Aβ‐PET‐related decline compared to the global composite score, indicating that a multidomain composite is more sensitive in detecting AD‐related decline. This finding aligns with previous research, suggesting that assessing multiple cognitive domains is the most effective way to capture the gradual progression seen in preclinical AD. 17 Supporting the utility of multidomain composite measures, our sample size analysis suggests that using a global composite score as an outcome in preclinical AD trials may be a key consideration in real‐world trial designs to minimize the sample size required to detect a treatment effect.

Supporting the utility of multidomain composite measures, our sample size analysis suggests that using a global composite score as an outcome in preclinical AD trials may be a key consideration in real‐world trial designs to minimize the sample size required to detect a treatment effect. Cognitive composite scores spanning multiple domains may increase sensitivity to subtle cognitive changes by minimizing measurement error and accounting for interindividual variability. At the group level, this improves statistical power, making such scores particularly effective for tracking cognitive decline in preclinical AD. 18 The feasibility of using a comprehensive composite score, compared to alternatives like extending the trial duration or using change in biomarkers as an outcome, 46 , 47 may vary depending on the trial's specific objectives and the available financial, personnel, and time resources. Raising biomarker thresholds for eligibility can be another effective strategy to decrease the number of participants needed to detect a treatment effect. While this strategy risks selecting individuals at more advanced disease stages, where interventions may be less effective, 48 in our case, the thresholds examined (e.g., 14, 24, and 34 Centiloids) remain within the early range of Aβ accumulation and still reflect evolving pathology. 49 Therefore, the concern about enrolling individuals too late in the disease process may be less relevant as even modest increases in inclusion thresholds could result in notable reductions in sample sizes. Overall, our findings illustrate that thoughtful selection of outcome measures and eligibility criteria can meaningfully influence trial feasibility, especially in CU populations.

Our finding of thresholds around 14 to 18 Centiloids, above which Aβ‐PET burden predicts cognitive decline in the total cohort and the MCI subsample, aligns with previous findings indicating that a Centiloid range of 15 to 18.5 is optimally predictive of future Aβ accumulation and cognitive decline. 4 , 50 While earlier studies used the PACC to identify this threshold, 4 in our study the PACC5 was least effective at capturing AD‐related decline. This difference may reflect variations in disease stage between cohorts. Cognitive decline measured by the PACC(5) has been shown to progress particularly rapidly in Aβ‐positive individuals who also exhibit elevated tau pathology, 33 in those who progress to MCI within 3 to 5 years, 51 and in individuals who have high Aβ burden, but not in those with intermediate Aβ levels. 21 , 22 These findings suggest that the PACC(5) is better suited to detect decline in later or more advanced stages of preclinical AD. In our CU participants, many are likely in earlier stages, which may explain the less pronounced decline, consistent with the low number of CU participants who converted to MCI ( n = 11). Additionally, most previous studies focused on CU samples with a mean age of 72 to 75 years, 20 , 32 , 33 , 51 which is considerably older than the mean of 65 years in our CU subsample. Additionally, most previous studies focused on CU samples with a mean age of 72 to 75 years, 20 , 32 , 33 , 51 which is considerably older than the mean of 65 years in our CU subsample. In both CU and MCI individuals, the lowest sample size estimates were observed when eligibility was based on a combination of cutoffs from Aβ SUVR and plasma p‐tau217 or plasma Aβ42/40 and p‐tau217. Among CU individuals, using any single biomarker alone resulted in sample size estimates > 5000 per arm. In MCI participants, estimates were substantially lower overall, and while the lowest values were observed with combined biomarker criteria as well, most single‐biomarker strategies, with the exception of plasma Aβ42/40 alone, resulted in similarly low sample size estimates. This observation aligns with previous research aimed at identifying Aβ‐PET‐positive individuals. These studies showed that adding plasma Aβ42/40 to a model already including plasma p‐tau217 did not significantly improve the detection of Aβ‐PET positivity in MCI participants but does enhance detection in CU individuals. 52 , 53 One likely explanation for the greater variability in sample size estimates among CU participants is the limited overlap between individuals meeting different biomarker cutoffs. For example, although 20 and 22 CU participants met the inclusion criteria for Aβ‐PET and p‐tau217 and Aβ42/40 and p‐tau217, respectively, only 13 individuals overlapped between these two groups. In MCI, by contrast, most individuals who met one inclusion criterion also met the others, resulting in more consistent sample size estimates. Finally, we found that, regardless of the inclusion criteria and composite score used, the average biomarker‐positive CU participant would still have a much higher score after 3 years compared to the average participant with MCI at baseline. Clinically, such a change is likely not meaningful. Nonetheless, it reflects early cognitive decline associated with underlying AD pathology and slowing this decline at such an early stage of the disease could lead to more substantial benefits over time, potentially delaying the onset of more severe cognitive deterioration. 54 Because several antibody‐based technologies exist for quantifying plasma biomarker levels, caution is needed when interpreting absolute threshold values. These values are comparable across studies using the same assay but not across different platforms. In addition, as shown in this work, cohort characteristics can strongly influence the derived thresholds, underscoring the need to establish context‐specific cutpoints for plasma biomarkers. 55 Nevertheless, in cohorts with similar characteristics, the pattern of results observed here is likely to generalize across assays, given the strong linear correlations reported between different p‐tau217 platforms. 56 , 57 , 58 Another important consideration is that the thresholds in this study were not intended to define underlying AD pathology but rather to optimize the prediction of future cognitive decline. Interestingly, like our Centiloid thresholds that align with commonly applied definitions of Aβ positivity, 49 the plasma p‐tau217 thresholds approximate previously observed cutoffs for distinguishing Aβ‐negative CU individuals from Aβ‐positive individuals. 59 This concordance is plausible, as early cognitive decline tends to emerge around the stage when Aβ pathology becomes reliably detectable with PET imaging. 4 , 49 A limitation of our study is the smaller MCI sample size, which limits the comparison of biomarker cutoffs across, but not within, (sub)cohorts.

A limitation of our study is the smaller MCI sample size, which limits the comparison of biomarker cutoffs across, but not within, (sub)cohorts. Additionally, the MCI cohort is not directly comparable to memory clinic‐based MCI cohorts. Furthermore, we observed a low correlation between plasma p‐tau217 levels and Aβ SUVR in the CU subsample, likely due to the low Aβ burden in many CU individuals and the number of participants with p‐tau217 levels below the detection threshold. Measurement methods of p‐tau217 vary in their ability to detect AD pathology, with mass spectrometry‐based approaches outperforming immunoassay‐based tests. 57 , 58 However, differences in the performance of plasma p‐tau217 across measurement methods are less pronounced when it comes to predicting cognitive decline, 58 and our results remain unchanged when participants with p‐tau217 levels below the detection threshold were excluded. Finally, we acknowledge that the biomarker thresholds were optimized for this cohort and have not been externally validated, which limits the generalizability of our findings. In conclusion, in individuals not specifically selected for memory or other cognitive disorders, AD‐related decline was most effectively captured by combining neuropsychological tasks across multiple cognitive domains, which substantially reduced the estimated sample size needed to detect treatment effects, particularly in cognitively unimpaired individuals. Additionally, combining plasma Aβ42/40 and p‐tau217 proved to be a valuable and practical method for identifying individuals at elevated risk of cognitive decline. Standardized and validated plasma biomarker thresholds are needed to reliably identify individuals at increased risk of cognitive decline.
